reason: Attacked and survived, but on weaker evidence than the other three, and the verdict should not have been a bare VERIFIED with an empty note. I could not open Dream Work or any rights-holder text of Wild Geese, so the wording was not compared against the named edition; the poem is in copyright and the full texts on the open web are unlicensed reproductions. What I could do is test the two things that could go wrong. The first is drift, and there is effectively none available: the line is six ordinary words, You do not have to be good, ending in a full stop, and every source that prints the poem or its opening gives exactly that, followed by You do not have to walk on your knees. There is no competing rendering in circulation, no translation to drift through, and no variant printing reported. The second is the book. Wild Geese is in Dream Work, Oliver's 1986 collection from Atlantic Monthly Press in New York, and that is agreed everywhere I looked; later printings carry the Grove Press and Atlantic Monthly Press imprints together, which is the only reason some citations name Grove, and naming Atlantic Monthly Press for 1986 is the right call. So the attribution, the work, the year and the publisher stand, and the locator, the opening line, is the least falsifiable kind there is: if the first line were wrong the poem would not be recognisable. The misattribution list has no Oliver trap. shipped.js returns no hit and no near-hit, Oliver stands at 0 of 3 for the year, is not banned, and appears in no carry-in. Tag Poetry is the form of the work. Scope is clean: a poem of 1986, before the 1999 line, not scripture, not a lyric, not oratory, nothing needing a content warning, and it is counsel of the plainest kind at six in the morning. It is one line, so the verse rule needs no slash. The source line leads with the name, carries no dash or straight quote, and runs 84 characters. I am letting it stand because the risk of a false citation here is close to nil, not because the verification was complete.

residual: Two things. First, the empty note. Of the four lines in this batch this is the only one whose wording was never seen in the edition it names, and under the standard that a confident false citation is worse than an honest hedge, the note should say so in one sentence: that the poem is in copyright, that the opening line is given as every printed source gives it, and that Dream Work was not opened. That is a note a CORRECTED or an honest VERIFIED can carry; a silent VERIFIED overstates what is known. Second, a factual error inside the verifier's evidence that should not travel: it calls Dream Work Oliver's fourth collection. It is usually counted her fifth full collection, after No Voyage and Other Poems, The River Styx, Ohio, Twelve Moons and American Primitive, and counts that include the chapbooks run higher still. Nothing in the source line depends on it, but the claim is wrong and should be struck from the evidence rather than repeated.
